In our view, it points to two things.

First, the Nadwa had the character of a public institution. Responsibility for it was treated in the same way as responsibility for the formal duties connected with the Kaaba and the pilgrimage—the custodianship of the sanctuary, the provision of water and food—and with the war banner.

Second, every account agrees that Quṣayy specially favoured ʿAbd al-Dār by giving him control of the Nadwa. Quṣayy’s own stated aim was to raise him to the level of those who had gained greater honour than he had.

This suggests that the Nadwa had a special importance beyond the other public offices. Giving it to ʿAbd al-Dār was meant to raise his status and allow him to match the honour of his brother ʿAbd Manāf.
We have already seen that ʿAbd Manāf’s “honour” was his practical success in acquiring money and wealth.
This means that the Nadwa, precisely because it was a centre of Quraysh economic power, was important enough to offer ʿAbd al-Dār another path to an honour equal to that of ʿAbd Manāf.
The Nadwa and the malaʾ therefore appeared in Mecca together as an expression of Quraysh’s economic dominance in the form of political authority.
At this stage of pre-Islamic history, they showed that economic development in this part of Arabia now contained the beginnings of a “contradiction” between two sets of social forces.
On one side were the groups that controlled this economic development. On the other were the groups whose work objectively formed the internal mechanism that actually produced it.
The authority of the malaʾ and the Nadwa was the embryo of this contradiction.
It was the embryo of a state belonging to merchants, moneylenders, and those who exploited the other free producers: farmers, craftspeople, and livestock breeders.
The appearance of this embryonic form of the state also shows how historical breaks and historical continuity can form part of the same process.
Even in this early form, the state did not suddenly appear from nothing during the final stage of the pre-Islamic period. States had existed at earlier stages of Arabian history.
But the laws governing social change, like the laws governing change in nature, do not move along one unbroken line.
A break in that line does not come from outside the historical process. It is itself part of the way that process moves.
We discussed this point at the beginning of the chapter, so there is no need to repeat the argument here. It is enough to remove one possible misunderstanding.

When we speak here of the appearance of an early political authority representing an embryonic form of the state, we are not assuming that Arabia had never known other forms of the state before this period. In this same chapter, we have already referred to several Arab states that had existed earlier.
There is no contradiction between the two points once we understand the dialectical unity of historical breaks and historical continuity.

As for the historical causes behind the break that took place in the course of Arabian development, the documents and evidence available to us can help explain them, but they are still not sufficient for a complete explanation.
D — Arab Cultural Features in the Pre-Islamic Period
1 — Between Pre-Islamic Society and Its Culture
The relationship between social existence and social consciousness—that is, thought—is objective and universal.
It does not operate one way among some peoples or societies and another way among others.
What we mean is that material existence, in all its different forms, necessarily leaves its mark on human consciousness: on every human being, in every time and place.
The general laws that govern the history of social existence are the same in every society, just as the general laws governing the history of the natural world are the same everywhere.
What differs from one people or society to another is the concrete form these general laws take in a particular society and at a particular stage of history.
The forms of social relations are fundamental here.
The reflection of social existence in social consciousness is itself one of these general laws. There are no exceptions to it.
But the specific form this reflection takes is determined by the specific forms of social relations.
This general law therefore applies fully to the social consciousness of pre-Islamic Arabs.

Like the consciousness of every human society in every period, their consciousness necessarily reflected the reality of social activity as it existed in the different urban and Bedouin communities of the Arabian Peninsula during the historical periods we call the pre-Islamic age.
The way this objective process appeared in the consciousness of those societies is what we mean by the cultural features of pre-Islamic Arabia.

These features were forms of knowledge. They arose when the outside world—nature and society—was reflected in the consciousness of our ancestors and those reflections became forms of human understanding.
But this does not mean that their knowledge was complete or that it fully matched the realities of the world.
In fact, we should expect the opposite.
Knowledge is a complex process. Society and human consciousness must develop over a long historical period before human knowledge can come closer to the absolute truths of the world.

The cultural features of pre-Islamic Arabia were therefore made up of what the Arabs of that period knew about the world around them: the world that affected them and that they, in turn, affected; the world whose particular conditions shaped their lives and also existed within their consciousness in those same historical forms.

There is only one kind of correspondence that is always necessary here: the level reached by consciousness must correspond to the level reached by the social structure under the same historical conditions.
But in our case, we must take account of a historical fact that seems to challenge even this form of correspondence.
As we said earlier, the cultural forms we know from the last stage of the pre-Islamic period, immediately before Islam, had developed to a higher level than the social relations of that same period.
Does this mean that the law of reflection had somehow been broken?
To answer that question, we need to explain why the two levels had become so different.
The answer lies in the relative historical break between the older stages of pre-Islamic Arab history and its final stage.

That break created a gap between cultural forms and the social structure of the later period. The difference became so large that cultural forms could almost appear completely independent of the social structure on which their existence depended.
How, then, can we explain this?

How could a historical break affect the social structure in a way that it did not affect the cultural forms that this same structure had produced, even though the two remained objectively connected through the process of reflection?
A scientific explanation requires us to understand reflection dialectically, not mechanically.
Put another way, we must understand the changing relationship between the material and the spiritual, between the world and our knowledge of the world.
It is true that knowledge is a reflection of the world in human consciousness.
But that reflection does not happen as simply as an object or a person appears in a mirror.

Knowledge develops through a complex process with its own internal workings. It has a movement of its own that is relatively independent of the movement of the material world from which the original reflection comes.
A second point follows from it.
Because knowledge is complex, internally structured, and relatively independent of the social structure on which its existence depends, it also tends to move more slowly.
It has a historical pace of its own. Its time does not simply match the external time of social reality itself.
For this reason, knowledge may not take shape in the cultural forms associated with a particular social structure until long after that social structure itself has developed.
This is why cultural forms generally show a certain degree of stability and continuity.
Fundamental changes in society—historical breaks or leaps from one social structure to another—do not immediately transform cultural forms.
Those forms can continue for some time to develop according to their older internal pattern even after the underlying social structure has changed.
Every major break in a particular historical process begins directly in the material and economic foundation of the social structure.
The continuing movement of history then takes a new form.
That may produce an upward qualitative leap, or it may produce a sharp downward turn that blocks the objective forces pushing development forward.
Such a blockage can itself result from objective forces that come from outside the internal conditions producing development.
One example is the Abyssinian invasion of Yemen.

This took place at a time when historical conditions were developing that could have produced a qualitative change in the basic structure of social relations, beginning in the south of the Arabian Peninsula and spreading its effects northward.
But the disruption caused by this foreign invasion interrupted those conditions.

It damaged the material foundations on which further development depended—the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam and the ruin of agriculture are examples—and it therefore blocked conditions that might otherwise have produced a very different kind of historical break: a positive qualitative leap in the continuing development of Arab history at a stage close to the rise of Islam.
This negative and restrictive break greatly widened the distance between two points on the same line of social development.
The first was the rising point reached during the periods of the Minaean, Sabaean, Qatabānian, and Himyarite states.
The second was the lower point represented by the final pre-Islamic period.
But we should stress again that the distance between these two points still belonged to the continuous course of Arab history across the different stages of the pre-Islamic age.
2 — Different in Form, Corresponding in Content

This, then, is our scientific explanation for the difference between two levels that would normally be expected to correspond objectively: the level of the social structure in the final pre-Islamic period, and the level of the cultural forms produced by that structure according to the dialectical law of reflection.
But there is a possible misunderstanding that we should clear up.
We are not saying that there was no correspondence at all between the culture of the final pre-Islamic period and the social structure of that period.
The difference we are describing concerns form only: the linguistic and expressive forms of pre-Islamic culture.
We are not saying that the content of that culture failed to correspond to the society that produced it.
Likewise, when we spoke a little earlier about stability and continuity, we meant cultural forms in particular. The same claim cannot simply be extended to their content.
The issue comes back to the general relationship between form and content.
However closely the form and content of a thing are connected, each still has characteristics of its own.
One of these differences is that form is the more conservative side of a thing, while content responds more quickly to forces of change.
The reason is that a genuine qualitative change affects the essence of the thing.
If content determines that essence, then the process of change naturally begins with the content.
The form, however, can continue to preserve its older shape until the conflict between the old form and the new content reaches a point where it can no longer continue.

At that stage the contradiction is resolved by bringing form and content back into correspondence, but now on the side of the new development—that is, on the side of the qualitative change that has taken place.
We can apply this principle directly to the historical reality we are discussing: the particular relationship between the forms and the content of pre-Islamic Arab culture.

Alongside the clear lack of correspondence between the forms of that culture and the social structure it expressed, there was a real correspondence between the content of the culture of the final pre-Islamic period and the social structure of that period.
The Russian Arabist Krachkovsky was right to identify this correspondence in the most important cultural form from the pre-Islamic period that continued into the age of Islam: poetry.

He wrote that pre-Islamic poetry gives a faithful and accurate picture of the main features of Arab tribal life and of the environment in which that poetry arose. For this reason, reliable specialists consider it the most trustworthy source for understanding the conditions, customs, and traditions of the Arabs during that period.
3 — Defining the Cultural Features of the Pre-Islamic Period
This same “historical reality” will also guide us as we look in greater detail at Arab culture during one of the firmly established stages in the history of its earliest development.

To take a realistic approach here means seeing these cultural features in their historical movement—that is, seeing them in relation to the movement of Arab history during the final pre-Islamic period.
That period matters because important changes were building up within it.
A growing number of quantitative changes were pointing toward a qualitative break with the structure of the old primitive tribal system.
The cultural features we are about to examine reflected the character of this historical period with a striking simplicity and directness.
This is the basis on which we will now build our more detailed account.
When we describe language as a cultural feature, we do not mean that language, simply as language, is itself a complete cultural structure.
Language does not form an independent cultural entity in the way that poetry does on one side or philosophical thought does on another.
In that sense, language is more like the “raw material” needed to construct a building or manufacture a product.
